title: Swiss meringue buttercream
summary: A silky, stable buttercream made by warming egg whites with sweetener over a water bath, whipping them to a meringue and beating in butter.

ingredients.note: softened but cool, cut into tablespoons

steps: Set a heatproof mixer bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, without the bowl touching the water. Make sure the bowl is completely free of grease.

Whisk the egg whites, erythritol, allulose and salt in the bowl until the mixture reaches 71 °C (160 °F) on a thermometer and feels smooth, not grainy, when rubbed between your fingers, about 5–8 minutes.
Move the bowl to the mixer and whip on high speed until the meringue is thick, glossy and the bowl feels cool, about 8–10 minutes.
Switch to medium speed and add the butter one piece at a time, waiting until each is mixed in.
If it looks curdled, keep beating: it comes together. If it stays soupy, chill the bowl 10 minutes and beat again; if it stays lumpy and cold, warm the side of the bowl briefly.
Beat in the vanilla. Use at once, or refrigerate up to a week and re-beat at room temperature before using.

swaps.note: firm stick style, not a tub spread

dairy_free_notes: Dairy-free butter makes a softer buttercream that loosens quickly in a warm room; chill the frosted cake to set it and pipe only in a cool kitchen.
tips: The allulose helps stop the erythritol from recrystallising into a gritty texture after chilling.
Butter that is too warm gives a soupy buttercream; it should dent with a finger but not look shiny.

origin.history: Meringue appears in French and English recipes by the 1600s and 1700s; the claim that it is named after the Swiss town of Meiringen is popular but unproven. Pastry cooks call a meringue whose whites and sugar are warmed together over a water bath 'Swiss', as a classification rather than a documented birthplace. Beating butter into it gives a stable buttercream that became a standard of twentieth-century cake decorating.
